subject: science
name: Electricity
summary: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge (I = Q/t), driven by a potential difference (V = W/Q). Ohm's law says V = IR for a conductor at constant temperature. Resistance depends on length, area and material (R = ρl/A). Resistors can be joined in series (R = R₁ + R₂ + …) or in parallel (1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …). Current produces heat (H = I²Rt), used in heaters, bulbs and fuses, and electric power is P = VI, with energy billed in kilowatt-hours.

topics.title: Electric current and circuits
topics.summary: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge, I = Q/t, measured in amperes with an ammeter connected in series. In metal wires, the moving charges are electrons.
topics.simple: Electric current is like the flow of water in a pipe, but what flows is electric charge. The more charge that passes a point each second, the bigger the current. We measure current in **amperes (A)** with an **ammeter**. A complete, unbroken path for current is called a **circuit**.
topics.explain:
**Electric current** is the amount of charge flowing through a cross-section of a conductor per unit time:

**I = Q/t**

- SI unit of charge: **coulomb (C)**
- SI unit of current: **ampere (A)**. 1 A = 1 C/s.
- Smaller units: 1 mA = 10⁻³ A; 1 µA = 10⁻⁶ A.

**Charge of an electron:** 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (negative). So 1 C is the charge of nearly **6 × 10¹⁸ electrons**.

**Direction of current:** by convention, current flows in the direction **opposite** to the flow of electrons, i.e. from the positive terminal to the negative terminal outside the cell. (This convention was chosen before electrons were discovered.)

**Electric circuit:** a continuous, closed path of an electric current. If the circuit is broken (for example, a switch is off), current stops and the bulb goes out.

**Ammeter:** measures current. It is always connected **in series** in the circuit.

**Common circuit symbols:** cell (a long thin line and a short thick line), battery (combination of cells), plug key or switch (open or closed), wire joint, wires crossing without joining, bulb, resistor, variable resistor (rheostat), ammeter, voltmeter.
topics.example:
A current of 0.5 A flows through a bulb for 10 minutes. How much charge passes?

t = 10 min = 600 s
Q = I × t = 0.5 × 600 = **300 C**

Number of electrons = 300 ÷ (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 1.9 × 10²¹ electrons.
keyPoints: I = Q/t; unit ampere (A) = coulomb per second
Charge of electron = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
1 C ≈ 6 × 10¹⁸ electrons
Conventional current: opposite to electron flow
Ammeter connected in series
Circuit must be closed for current to flow

topics.title: Electric potential and potential difference
topics.summary: Charges flow when there is a potential difference between two points. Potential difference is the work done per unit charge, V = W/Q, measured in volts with a voltmeter connected in parallel.
topics.simple: Water flows only if there's a height difference. In the same way, charge flows only if there's a **potential difference** (voltage). A cell creates this difference using chemical energy. Potential difference tells how much work is done to move each coulomb of charge. It's measured in **volts (V)** with a **voltmeter**.
topics.explain:
Charges do not flow on their own in a wire, just as water in a perfectly level pipe doesn't flow. They move only if there is a **difference of electric pressure**, called the **potential difference**.

A **cell or battery** produces this potential difference using the **chemical reaction** inside it. It does work to keep the charges moving around the circuit.

**Definition:** the electric potential difference between two points is the **work done to move a unit charge** from one point to the other:

**V = W/Q**

- SI unit: **volt (V)**
- **1 volt** is the potential difference when **1 joule** of work is done to move **1 coulomb** of charge: 1 V = 1 J/C.

**Voltmeter:** measures potential difference. It is always connected **in parallel** across the two points.

**Summary of connections:**
- Ammeter → series (it measures what flows through)
- Voltmeter → parallel (it compares two points)
topics.example:
How much work is done in moving 2 C of charge across two points with a potential difference of 12 V?

W = V × Q = 12 × 2 = **24 J**

Another: if 60 J of work moves 5 C between two points, V = W/Q = 60 ÷ 5 = **12 V**.
keyPoints: Charge flows only when there is a potential difference
V = W/Q; unit volt (V) = joule per coulomb
Cell creates potential difference by chemical reaction
Voltmeter connected in parallel
1 V = 1 J of work per 1 C of charge

topics.title: Ohm's law, resistance and resistivity
topics.summary: Ohm's law: at constant temperature, current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, V = IR. Resistance depends on length, cross-sectional area and material: R = ρl/A, where ρ is resistivity.
topics.simple: Georg Ohm found that if you double the voltage across a wire, the current doubles too, as long as the temperature stays the same. So V = IR. **Resistance (R)** is how much a material opposes current. A long, thin wire has more resistance than a short, thick one. Copper and aluminium have low resistance, so they're used for wires; nichrome has high resistance, so it's used in heaters.
topics.explain:
**Ohm's law:** the potential difference V across a metallic wire is **directly proportional** to the current I through it, provided its **temperature remains the same**.

V ∝ I → **V = IR**

The V–I graph is a **straight line through the origin**; its slope gives R.

**Resistance (R):** the property of a conductor to resist the flow of charges. SI unit **ohm (Ω)**. 1 Ω is the resistance of a conductor when a potential difference of 1 V across it gives a current of 1 A.

I = V/R, so for a fixed voltage, current is **inversely proportional** to resistance. A **rheostat** (variable resistance) is used to change current in a circuit.

**Factors affecting resistance:**
- Directly proportional to **length**: R ∝ l
- Inversely proportional to **area of cross-section**: R ∝ 1/A
- Depends on the **nature of the material**
- Depends on **temperature**

Combining: **R = ρ l / A**

**ρ (rho)** is the **resistivity** of the material, its characteristic property. SI unit: **Ω m**.
- Metals and alloys have very low resistivity: about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω m. They are good **conductors**.
- Insulators such as rubber and glass have very high resistivity: about 10¹² to 10¹⁷ Ω m.
- Resistivity of a material changes with temperature.
- **Alloys** have higher resistivity than their constituent metals and **don't oxidise (burn) easily** at high temperatures. That's why **nichrome** is used in heaters, toasters and irons.
- **Copper and aluminium** are used for transmission and household wiring because of their **low resistivity**.
- **Tungsten** is used almost exclusively for bulb filaments.
topics.deep:
**Effect of changes on resistance:**
- Length doubled → R doubled
- Area doubled → R halved
- Diameter halved → area becomes ¼ (A = πr²) → R becomes 4 times
- Wire stretched to double length (volume fixed) → length × 2 and area ÷ 2 → R becomes 4 times
topics.example:
**Example 1 (Ohm's law):** a bulb draws 0.5 A from a 220 V supply. Its resistance is R = V/I = 220 ÷ 0.5 = **440 Ω**.

**Example 2 (current):** a heater of resistance 44 Ω is connected to 220 V. I = V/R = 220 ÷ 44 = **5 A**.

**Example 3 (resistivity):** a wire of resistance 10 Ω is stretched to twice its length without changing its volume. Its area halves, so R = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4 × ρl/A = 4 × 10 = **40 Ω**.
keyPoints: Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature
V–I graph is a straight line through the origin
R ∝ l and R ∝ 1/A, so R = ρl/A
Resistivity ρ depends on material and temperature; unit Ω m
Alloys (nichrome) have high resistivity → heating elements
Copper, aluminium (low ρ) → wires; tungsten → bulb filaments

topics.title: Resistors in series and parallel
topics.summary: In series, the same current flows through each resistor and R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃. In parallel, each resistor has the same potential difference and 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃. Homes use parallel circuits.
topics.simple: Resistors in **series** are joined end to end, in one line. The same current goes through all of them, and their resistances simply add up. Resistors in **parallel** are joined side by side. Each gets the full voltage, and the total resistance becomes **less** than the smallest one. Your home's lights and fans are connected in parallel so each one works on its own.
topics.explain:
**Series combination** (end to end):
- The **same current** flows through every resistor.
- The total potential difference equals the **sum** of the potential differences across each: V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃.
- Equivalent resistance: **Rs = R₁ + R₂ + R₃**. It is **greater** than any single resistor.

**Parallel combination** (side by side, between the same two points):
- The **potential difference** across each resistor is the **same**.
- The total current equals the **sum** of the currents through each: I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃.
- Equivalent resistance: **1/Rp = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃**. It is **less** than the smallest single resistor.

**Why homes use parallel, not series:**
- In series, if one appliance fails or is switched off, the circuit breaks and **all** stop working.
- In series, the current is the same through all, but appliances need **different currents** (a heater needs much more than a bulb).
- In series, the total resistance becomes large, so current falls.
- In **parallel**, each appliance gets the **full voltage**, can be switched on and off independently, and draws the current it needs.
keyPoints: Series: same current; V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃
Series: Rs = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ (bigger than each)
Parallel: same voltage; I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃
Parallel: 1/Rp = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ (smaller than smallest)
Two equal resistors R in parallel give R/2
Household circuits are wired in parallel

topics.title: Heating effect of electric current
topics.summary: When current flows through a resistor, electrical energy is turned into heat. Joule's law: H = I²Rt. It is used in heaters, irons, toasters, bulbs and fuses, but is unwanted in computers and wires.
topics.simple: When current passes through a wire, the wire gets hot. The heat produced depends on the current, the resistance and the time: **H = I²Rt**. Doubling the current makes four times the heat. We use this in electric irons, kettles, heaters, bulbs and fuses.
topics.explain:
When a source drives current through a purely resistive circuit, the energy supplied is **dissipated entirely as heat**. This is the **heating effect of electric current**.

Work done to move charge Q through potential difference V: W = VQ. With Q = It and V = IR, the heat produced is:

**H = VIt = I²Rt**

**Joule's law of heating:** the heat produced in a resistor is:
- directly proportional to the **square of the current** (H ∝ I²),
- directly proportional to the **resistance** (H ∝ R),
- directly proportional to the **time** for which current flows (H ∝ t).

**Useful applications:**
- **Electric iron, toaster, oven, kettle, room heater:** heating elements made of high-resistivity alloys like nichrome
- **Electric bulb:** the **tungsten** filament (melting point 3380 °C) gets so hot that it glows and gives light. Bulbs are filled with chemically inactive **nitrogen and argon** to make the filament last longer. Much of the energy still comes out as heat.
- **Electric fuse:** a wire of a metal or alloy with a suitable **low melting point** (e.g. aluminium, copper, iron, lead). If a current larger than the rating flows, the fuse wire **melts** and breaks the circuit, protecting appliances. It is connected **in series** with the device. Fuses for home use are rated 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A, etc.

**Unwanted effect:** heating wastes energy in wires and can damage parts in computers and other devices, which is why some need cooling fans.
topics.example:
A current of 2 A flows through a 20 Ω resistor for 30 s. Heat produced:
H = I²Rt = 2² × 20 × 30 = 4 × 20 × 30 = **2400 J**

**Choosing a fuse:** an electric iron uses 1 kW at 220 V. Current I = P/V = 1000 ÷ 220 ≈ 4.5 A. So a **5 A** fuse is suitable.
keyPoints: H = I²Rt (Joule's law of heating)
Heat ∝ I², ∝ R, ∝ t
Heating elements use nichrome (high resistivity, doesn't oxidise easily)
Bulb filament: tungsten (melting point 3380 °C); bulb filled with nitrogen and argon
Fuse: low melting point wire in series; melts on excess current
Unwanted heating wastes energy in wires and devices

topics.title: Electric power and energy
topics.summary: Electric power is the rate of using electrical energy: P = VI = I²R = V²/R, measured in watts. Commercial energy is measured in kilowatt-hours (units): 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
topics.simple: Power tells how fast an appliance uses electrical energy. A 1000 W heater uses energy ten times faster than a 100 W bulb. **P = VI**. Your electricity bill counts energy in **units**, where 1 unit = 1 **kilowatt-hour (kWh)**: using 1000 W for 1 hour.
topics.explain:
**Electric power** is the rate at which electric energy is consumed (or dissipated):

**P = VI**

Using Ohm's law, this can also be written as:
- **P = I²R**
- **P = V²/R**

**SI unit:** **watt (W)**. 1 W is the power used by a device that carries 1 A at 1 V: 1 W = 1 V × 1 A = 1 J/s.
- 1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W

**Electrical energy:** E = P × t

The joule is too small for household use, so the commercial unit is the **kilowatt-hour (kWh)**, often called one **'unit'** on the electricity bill.

**1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J**

**Power rating:** an appliance marked '220 V, 1100 W' uses 1100 W when connected to 220 V. From this, you can find:
- current: I = P/V = 1100 ÷ 220 = 5 A
- resistance: R = V²/P = 220² ÷ 1100 = 48400 ÷ 1100 = 44 Ω

Note: an electric bill charges for **energy (kWh)**, not for power or for current. 'Electricity' is not consumed in the sense of charge being used up; energy is.
topics.example:
A 1000 W heater runs 2 hours a day for 30 days. Electricity costs ₹8 per unit.

Energy = P × t = 1 kW × (2 × 30) h = **60 kWh = 60 units**
Cost = 60 × ₹8 = **₹480**

Another: a 100 W bulb and a 60 W bulb both on 220 V. The 100 W bulb draws I = 100/220 ≈ 0.45 A; the 60 W bulb draws 60/220 ≈ 0.27 A. The 60 W bulb has the higher resistance: R = 220²/60 ≈ 807 Ω, versus 220²/100 = 484 Ω for the 100 W bulb.
keyPoints: P = VI = I²R = V²/R
Unit of power: watt (W) = 1 J/s
Energy E = P × t
1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
Power rating tells P at the stated voltage
Bills charge for energy in kWh

commonMistakes: Connecting a voltmeter in series or an ammeter in parallel. Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel.
Forgetting to convert time to seconds in Q = It or H = I²Rt.
Adding resistances directly in parallel. Use 1/Rp = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …, then take the reciprocal at the end.
Forgetting the final step in parallel problems: 1/Rp = 10/30 means Rp = 3 Ω, not 0.33 Ω.
Thinking heat ∝ I. Heat is proportional to I², so doubling current gives four times the heat.
Thinking a 100 W bulb has more resistance than a 60 W bulb. At the same voltage, the higher-power bulb has lower resistance (R = V²/P).
Thinking the conventional current flows the same way as electrons. It is opposite to electron flow.
Confusing resistance with resistivity. Resistance depends on shape and size; resistivity depends only on the material (and temperature).

Tungsten filament; bulbs filled with nitrogen and argon.

faqs.q: What is the difference between resistance and resistivity?
faqs.a: **Resistance** (R, in Ω) depends on the wire's length, thickness, material and temperature. **Resistivity** (ρ, in Ω m) depends only on the material and temperature, not on its size or shape. They are linked by R = ρl/A.

faqs.q: Why are household appliances connected in parallel?
faqs.a: In parallel, each appliance gets the full 220 V, can be switched on or off independently, and draws its own required current. In series, one switched-off appliance would break the circuit for all, and the total resistance would be too high.

faqs.q: Why is nichrome used in heaters instead of copper?
faqs.a: Nichrome is an alloy with **high resistivity**, so it produces a lot of heat (H = I²Rt), and it **does not oxidise (burn) easily** at high temperatures. Copper has low resistivity, so it is used for connecting wires instead.

faqs.q: Why is a fuse connected in series?
faqs.a: So that all the current to the appliance passes through it. If the current becomes too large, the fuse wire melts and breaks the whole circuit, cutting off the supply and protecting the appliance.

faqs.q: What does '1 unit' of electricity mean on the bill?
faqs.a: One unit is **1 kilowatt-hour (kWh)**: the energy used by a 1000 W appliance running for 1 hour. 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
